header: PROTECTING AMERICANS FROM TAX HIKES ACT OF 2015
summary:
This division is a tax-law package, not a department spending bill. It does not appropriate a lump sum to an agency. Dollar figures below are the limits, rates, and thresholds written into the statute, not budget scores. The text does not include an official revenue estimate.

## Overview

Division Q is the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes Act of 2015. It amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. Its purpose is to extend, and in many cases make permanent, temporary tax breaks that had been renewed year to year, and to tighten rules meant to reduce improper claims of refundable credits. It also changes rules for real estate investment trusts, retirement accounts, the IRS, and a few trade and excise-tax items.

## Total Spending

No total appropriation is stated. This division changes tax rules rather than funding a department. Title VI is labeled “Budgetary Effects,” but the excerpt does not include a dollar total or a revenue score. Any 10-year cost figure would have to come from a separate official estimate, not from this text.

## Key Funding Areas

These are tax benefits and limits, not agency budgets:

- **Child tax credit (refundable portion)**: earned-income threshold kept at **$3,000** instead of rising to **$10,000** — made permanent, so lower-income families can still receive the refundable credit.
- **Earned income tax credit**: higher rate for families with 3 or more children (**45%**) and a **$5,000** increase in the income level where the credit starts to phase out for married couples — made permanent and adjusted for inflation.
- **American opportunity tax credit**: the enhanced college credit is made permanent (it had been scheduled to end before 2018).
- **Teacher classroom-expense deduction**: **$250** a year made permanent, later adjusted for inflation, and expanded to include some professional-development costs.
- **Transit and parking benefits**: the monthly tax-free transit benefit is raised from **$100** to **$175**, matching parking.
- **State and local sales-tax deduction**: made permanent for people who deduct sales taxes instead of state income taxes.
- **Research credit**: the business research credit is made permanent. Eligible small startups can apply up to **$250,000** of the credit against payroll taxes. A “qualified small business” generally has gross receipts under **$5 million**.
- **Section 179 expensing**: businesses can immediately deduct up to **$500,000** of equipment and certain property, phasing out after **$2 million** of purchases — made permanent and inflation-adjusted. Air-conditioning and heating units can qualify.
- **Bonus depreciation**: extended through 2019 and phased down. The extra first-year write-off for passenger cars is **$8,000**, then **$6,400** in 2018 and **$4,800** in 2019.
- **Medical device excise tax**: suspended for sales from **January 1, 2016, through December 31, 2017**.

## Notable Provisions

**Made permanent (among others)**
- Enhanced child tax credit, earned income credit, and American opportunity credit.
- Deduction for state and local general sales taxes.
- Parity between employer-paid transit and parking benefits.
- Charitable breaks for conservation easements, IRA gifts to charity, and donated food inventory (generally capped at **15%** of relevant income). Alaska Native Corporations get a special conservation-contribution rule.
- Research credit; 15-year write-off for certain leasehold, restaurant, and retail improvements; 100% exclusion of gain on certain small-business stock; a 5-year recognition period for S-corporation built-in gains; the active-financing exception; and a minimum rate for the low-income housing credit. Military housing allowances can continue to be ignored in certain low-income housing income tests.

**Extended through 2019**
- New markets tax credit (unused authority can be carried into 2024).
- Work opportunity credit, including a new category for people unemployed at least **27** straight weeks.
- Bonus depreciation, stepping down after 2017 (generally 50%, then 40% in 2018 and 30% in 2019).
- Look-through treatment of certain payments between related foreign subsidiaries, through January 1, 2020.

**Extended through 2016**
- Exclusion for forgiven mortgage debt on a principal home, deduction for mortgage insurance premiums, and the above-the-line tuition deduction.
- A long list of narrower breaks: Indian employment credit, railroad track maintenance, mine rescue training, qualified zone academy bonds, certain race horses treated as 3-year property, motorsports complexes, faster depreciation on Indian reservations, mine-safety equipment, film and TV expensing (expanded to some live theater), Puerto Rico production activities, empowerment zones, a higher rum-tax “cover over” for Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, and the American Samoa economic-development credit.
- Energy items, including credits for home energy improvements, alternative-fuel pumps, two-wheeled plug-in vehicles, biodiesel and renewable diesel, second-generation biofuel, Indian coal, certain renewable-electricity facilities, energy-efficient new homes, and energy-efficient commercial buildings.

**Program integrity**
- Wage and nonemployee-compensation forms generally due **January 31**.
- Refunds that include the earned income credit or the refundable child tax credit cannot be paid before **February 15**.
- Small dollar errors on information returns need not be corrected if no single error exceeds **$100**, or **$25** for tax withheld.
- New rules for individual taxpayer identification numbers (ITINs), including expiration if unused and stricter application rules.
- No retroactive claims of the earned income credit, child tax credit, or American opportunity credit based on a Social Security or taxpayer ID number issued after the return due date.
- Paid-preparer due-diligence rules extended to the child tax credit and American opportunity credit. Willful or reckless preparer penalty rises from **50%** to **75%**. Fraudulent credit claims can bar the credit for **10** years; reckless claims for **2** years.
- Colleges must report tuition actually paid, and the American opportunity credit requires the school’s employer identification number.

**Other notable changes**
- 529 college accounts: computers and internet access can be qualified expenses; refunded tuition can be put back into the account within **60 days**.
- ABLE disability accounts: the requirement that the program be in the beneficiary’s home state is dropped.
- Civil damages and similar awards to wrongfully incarcerated people are excluded from income. Claims for past years can be filed within one year of enactment.
- Early-retirement-distribution relief extended to nuclear materials couriers, U.S. Capitol Police, Supreme Court Police, and State Department diplomatic security agents.
- Tax-collection time limits are not extended merely because a service member is hospitalized for combat-zone injuries.
- REIT spin-offs are restricted. The share of REIT assets that can sit in taxable REIT subsidiaries falls from **25%** to **20%** for years beginning after 2017. Withholding on many sales of U.S. real property interests by foreigners rises from **10%** to **15%**, but stays **10%** for a residence if the amount realized does not exceed **$1 million**. Foreign pension funds get a FIRPTA exception.
- Small insurance companies: the alternative-tax premium cap rises from **$1.2 million** to **$2.2 million**, with new diversification tests, for years beginning after 2016.
- For 2016 only, certain corporate timber gains can be taxed at **23.8%**.
- “Hard cider” is redefined (including cider under **8.5%** alcohol, with limits on carbonation and fruit flavoring).
- IRS: employees must follow a listed set of taxpayer rights; personal email cannot be used for official business; new 501(c)(4) groups must notify the IRS within **60 days** (failure penalty up to **$5,000**); gift tax does not apply to contributions to certain 501(c)(4), (c)(5), and (c)(6) groups. The text is cut off in the middle of the partnership-audit rules.
- Trade items listed in the table of contents — a tariff-classification date for recreational outerwear and an Asia-Pacific agreement on duties for certain environmental goods — are not spelled out in the excerpt provided.

## Who Benefits

- **Lower- and moderate-income families with children**, through the permanent earned income credit and refundable child tax credit.
- **College students and families saving for college**, through the American opportunity credit, the tuition deduction (through 2016), and easier 529 and ABLE rules.
- **Teachers**, through the permanent **$250** classroom deduction.
- **Commuters**, through equal tax-free transit and parking benefits.
- **People in states with no or low income taxes**, who can keep deducting state and local sales taxes.
- **Homeowners**, through temporary relief on forgiven mortgage debt and mortgage-insurance premiums.
- **Businesses that invest, do research, or hire**, especially small firms using section 179, the research credit, bonus depreciation, and the work opportunity credit, including employers who hire the long-term unemployed.
- **Charities, food banks, and land-conservation groups**, through permanent giving incentives.
- **Real estate investors, REITs, and some foreign pension funds**, through housing-credit and FIRPTA changes.
- **Specific industries and places**, including film and live theater, railroads, mines, motorsports, horse racing, tribes and Indian reservations, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, renewable fuels, and medical-device makers during the tax suspension.
- **Wrongfully incarcerated people** and certain federal law-enforcement and military personnel, through narrow exclusions and retirement rules.
- **The IRS and compliant taxpayers**, through earlier wage reporting, delayed refunds, and tighter ID and preparer rules intended to cut improper credit claims.

## Plain English Summary

This part of the bill is not a check to a federal department. It is a big tax deal that stops a long list of tax breaks from expiring and makes the best-known family credits permanent, so parents, students, teachers, and commuters are not waiting each December to see if Congress will renew them. Businesses also keep write-offs for equipment and research, and a pile of narrower breaks — from biodiesel to racehorses to rum taxes in Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands — get another year or two. In exchange, the IRS gets tougher tools on refundable credits: wage forms come in sooner, some refunds are held until mid-February, and people cannot claim those credits retroactively with an ID number issued after the filing deadline. The bill does not say, in this text, how many dollars of federal revenue all of that gives up.

titles.summary:
This title does not appropriate money to agencies. It amends the Internal Revenue Code to make some expiring tax provisions permanent and to extend others through 2016 or 2019.

## Title Summary

Title I (the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes Act of 2015 portion of Division Q) extends or locks in individual, charitable, business, real-estate, and energy tax provisions. It does not fund a bureau or program. Subtitle A makes selected breaks permanent; Subtitle B extends several through 2019; Subtitle C extends a larger set through 2016, including a two-year pause in the medical device excise tax.

## Spending Breakdown

These are statutory tax parameters in the text, not appropriated outlays. The title states no agency budget totals or revenue scores.

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Refundable child tax credit earned-income threshold | $3,000 (replaces $10,000) | Permanently keeps the lower threshold for the additional child tax credit |
| EITC joint-return phaseout increase | $5,000 (inflation-adjusted after 2015) | Permanently reduces the marriage penalty in the earned income credit |
| Educator expense deduction | $250 (indexed after 2015; increases rounded to $50) | Permanent above-the-line deduction; later expanded to certain professional development |
| Transit fringe parity | $175 (replaces $100) | Permanent parity between mass-transit and parking exclusions |
| Research credit against payroll tax (startups) | Up to $250,000; gross receipts under $5,000,000 | Lets certain new small businesses apply the research credit to employer FICA |
| Section 179 expensing | $500,000 limit; phaseout begins at $2,000,000 (indexed after 2015, rounded to $10,000) | Permanent higher expensing for qualifying business property, including software and certain real property |
| Bonus depreciation — passenger automobiles | +$8,000; $6,400 in 2018; $4,800 in 2019 | Extra first-year depreciation cap while bonus depreciation phases down |
| Certain aircraft (bonus depreciation) | Deposit of 10% or $100,000, whichever is less; cost over $200,000 | Special placed-in-service rule for qualifying aircraft |
| Food-inventory charitable deduction | 15% of applicable income; elective basis of 25% of fair market value | Permanent enhanced deduction, with limits and basis rules for some donors |
| New markets tax credit | Years only: allocations for 2010–2019; unused limitation carryover through 2024 | Extends the credit; this text does not restate the annual dollar cap |
| Medical device excise tax | No tax on sales from Jan. 1, 2016, through Dec. 31, 2017 | Two-year moratorium, not a repeal |

## Notable Sections

- **Permanent family credits (Secs. 101–103):** Locks in the enhanced child tax credit refundability threshold, the American opportunity tax credit, and the larger EITC for families with three or more children (credit percentage 45; phaseout percentage 21.06), plus the $5,000 joint-return adjustment.
- **Research credit (Sec. 121):** Makes the credit permanent, allows it against the alternative minimum tax for eligible small businesses, and lets qualifying startups offset up to $250,000 of employer Social Security tax.
- **Section 179 and bonus depreciation (Secs. 124, 143):** Permanently sets expensing at $500,000 / $2,000,000 and extends 50 percent bonus depreciation, phasing to 40 percent in 2018 and 30 percent in 2019. Adds qualified improvement property and a special rule for certain fruit- and nut-bearing plants.
- **Narrow or contested extenders:** Active-financing exception from subpart F (Sec. 128, permanent); CFC look-through through 2019 (Sec. 144); 100 percent exclusion for certain small-business stock (Sec. 126); 3-year recovery for certain race horses and 7-year recovery for motorsports complexes through 2016 (Secs. 165–166); rum excise-tax cover-over to Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands through 2016 (Sec. 172).
- **New or expanded rules:** Charitable conservation contributions by Alaska Native Corporations (Sec. 111); work opportunity credit for people unemployed at least 27 consecutive weeks (Sec. 142, for work begun after 2015); expensing for qualified live theatrical productions in venues of not more than 3,000 seats, or 6,500 for short seasonal runs (Sec. 169).
- **Medical device tax (Sec. 174):** Suspends the excise tax on sales in 2016 and 2017.
- **Retroactive energy claims (Secs. 185, 192):** Directs Treasury to allow one-time claims for 2015 biodiesel and alternative-fuel credits, with guidance, a 180-day filing window, and payment generally within 60 days.

## Plain English

Instead of giving agencies new budgets, this title keeps or temporarily continues tax breaks that lower taxes for many families, charities, businesses, real-estate investors, and energy producers.

This title does not appropriate money. It amends the Internal Revenue Code to tighten compliance for wage reporting and for the earned income tax credit (EITC), child tax credit (CTC), and American opportunity tax credit (AOTC), and to restrict how individual taxpayer identification numbers (ITINs) are issued and kept.

## Spending Breakdown

No line-item appropriations appear in this title. The only dollar figures are compliance thresholds and a penalty rate.

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| De minimis dollar-amount error safe harbor | $100 | Information returns and payee statements need not be corrected if no single incorrect amount is off by more than $100 |
| De minimis withholding-error safe harbor | $25 | Same safe harbor if tax withheld is not off by more than $25 |
| Paid-preparer willful or reckless penalty | Raised from 50% to 75% of income derived | Higher penalty under IRC §6694(b) for returns prepared for years ending after enactment |

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 201** moves Forms W–2, W–3, and nonemployee-compensation statements to a January 31 filing deadline and bars EITC and additional CTC refunds before February 15 (refund rule applies to credits or refunds made after December 31, 2016).
- **Sec. 202** creates the $100/$25 safe harbor for small dollar errors on information returns and payee statements (returns and statements required after December 31, 2016). The recipient can elect out of the payee-statement safe harbor.
- **Sec. 203** codifies ITIN rules: in-person or mail application with original or certified identity documents; numbers expire after three consecutive years with no tax return (or dependent listing); pre-2013 ITINs phase out on a schedule from January 1, 2017, through January 1, 2020. Requires a community-based certified acceptance-agent program, a Treasury study (report within 1 year), and TIGTA audits every 2 years. Expired or invalid ITINs can be treated as math errors.
- **Secs. 204–206** block retroactive claims of the EITC, CTC, and AOTC if the required taxpayer identification number was issued after the return due date. Timely original 2015 returns are excepted; later amendments are not.
- **Sec. 207** extends paid-preparer due-diligence rules and the related penalty from the EITC to the CTC and AOTC (taxable years beginning after December 31, 2015) and orders a Treasury study of those rules.
- **Sec. 208** bars the CTC and AOTC for 10 years after a final determination of fraud, and for 2 years after reckless or intentional disregard. A prior deficiency denial requires the taxpayer to re-prove eligibility before claiming the credit again.
- **Secs. 209–210** apply the erroneous-claim penalty to the EITC, switch that penalty’s exception from “reasonable basis” to “reasonable cause,” and raise the willful/reckless preparer penalty from 50% to 75% of income derived.
- **Secs. 211–212** require the school’s employer identification number for the AOTC and limit education information reporting to qualified tuition and related expenses actually paid, not amounts billed.

## Plain English

The IRS must get wage forms earlier, hold some EITC and child-credit refunds until mid-February, and make it harder to claim those credits—or keep an ITIN—without a timely, valid identification number.

This title does not appropriate program funding. It amends the Internal Revenue Code through four subtitles of tax rules, mostly in the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes Act of 2015 (Division Q of H.R. 2029).

## Title Summary

Title III—Miscellaneous Provisions changes tax treatment for education savings, disability accounts, wrongful-incarceration awards, retirement plans, real estate investment trusts (REITs), and a set of excise, charitable, insurance, timber, and energy rules. It does not fund a named agency or bureau. The operative agencies are the Internal Revenue Service (for administration and withholding) and, in limited cases, the Treasury Department (for regulations and a small payment tied to clean-coal grants).

## Spending Breakdown

There are no appropriation line items or agency funding totals in this title. Dollar figures below are statutory thresholds, rates, or limits in the tax rules, not spending.

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| FIRPTA withholding on U.S. real property dispositions (sec. 324) | Rate raised from 10% to 15% | Higher withholding on certain sales by foreign persons; 10% kept for a residence if the amount realized does not exceed $1,000,000 |
| Small-producer alcohol excise filing (sec. 332) | Not more than $1,000 / not more than $50,000 | Longer payment periods and bond relief for very small distilled-spirits, wine, and beer taxpayers |
| Small insurance company alternative tax (sec. 333) | Premium cap raised from $1,200,000 to $2,200,000 | More companies may use the alternative tax; cap later adjusted for inflation in $50,000 steps |
| Taxable REIT subsidiary asset cap (sec. 312) | Reduced from 25% to 20% | Tighter limit on REIT assets held in taxable subsidiaries, for years beginning after 2017 |
| Qualified timber gain corporate rate (sec. 334) | 23.8% on the least of timber gain, net capital gain, or taxable income | One-year (2016) special rate for certain long-held timber; remainder taxed at 35% |
| Clean-coal grant exclusion (sec. 343) | Payment equal to 1.18% of the grant | Noncorporate recipients may exclude certain Energy Policy Act grants if they pay this amount to Treasury |

## Notable Sections

- **New or expanded exclusions (Subtitle A).** Sec. 301 excludes work-college program amounts from income. Sec. 302 permanently treats computers, software, and internet access as qualified 529 expenses, drops distribution-aggregation rules, and allows 60-day recontribution of refunded education expenses. Sec. 303 drops the state-residency requirement for ABLE disability accounts. Sec. 304 creates a new exclusion (sec. 139F) for civil damages, restitution, and similar awards to wrongfully incarcerated people, and waives the statute of limitations for one year so earlier years can be refunded.
- **Retirement and military rules.** Sec. 306 allows rollovers into SIMPLE accounts after the two-year period. Sec. 308 extends the early-distribution exception to nuclear materials couriers, U.S. Capitol Police, Supreme Court Police, and State Department diplomatic security agents. Sec. 309 stops combat-zone hospitalization from extending the IRS collection period after assessment.
- **REIT restrictions and FIRPTA (Subtitle B).** Sec. 311 generally blocks tax-free spinoffs if either company is a REIT and bars a REIT election for 10 years after certain spinoffs (with limited exceptions; applies to distributions on or after December 7, 2015, with a ruling-request carve-out). Secs. 322–323 ease FIRPTA for larger holders of publicly traded REIT stock, certain “qualified shareholders,” and qualified foreign pension funds. Sec. 324 raises FIRPTA withholding from 10% to 15%.
- **Other targeted rules (Subtitles C and D).** Sec. 331 treats gifts to certain agricultural research organizations like other public-charity contributions. Sec. 333 adds diversification and reporting rules for small insurers using the alternative tax. Sec. 335 broadens the definition of hard cider (apples or pears; under 8.5% alcohol). Sec. 336 clarifies church-plan controlled-group, transfer, automatic-enrollment, and collective-trust rules, including preemption of conflicting state payroll laws for church-plan automatic enrollment. Sec. 345 denies loss-duplication treatment when the prior disallowed loss belonged to a party that would not have paid U.S. income tax on it.

## Plain English

This title does not send money to a federal agency; it changes who owes tax, and how much, on education savings, disability accounts, wrongful-conviction awards, real-estate investment trusts, foreign real-estate sales, and a handful of smaller business and energy items.

This title does not appropriate money. It changes how the IRS and the U.S. Tax Court operate, mainly by codifying taxpayer rights, tightening rules for tax-exempt organizations, and adjusting court procedures.

## Title Summary

Title IV—Tax Administration (Division Q) amends the Internal Revenue Code and related court rules. Subtitle A covers Internal Revenue Service conduct, disclosure, exempt-organization procedures, partnership audits, and credentials. Subtitle B covers taxpayer access to the U.S. Tax Court and the Court’s administration and status. It creates duties, penalties, and procedures; it does not fund agencies or programs.

## Spending Breakdown

No appropriation or spending line items appear in this title. Dollar figures in the text are penalties or case thresholds, not funding:

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Appropriations | None | No funds are provided for the IRS, Tax Court, or any program |
| 501(c)(4) notice penalty (organization) | $20 per day, not to exceed $5,000 per notice | Penalty for failing to notify the IRS of intent to operate as a 501(c)(4) |
| 501(c)(4) notice penalty (managers) | $20 per day after written demand, not to exceed $5,000 per notice | Penalty on persons who still fail to submit the notice after IRS demand |
| 501(c)(4) notice user fee | “Reasonable” fee; amount not set | Fee for the notice; may be spent only if an appropriations act provides for it |
| Small tax case election (interest abatement) | Abatement sought does not exceed $50,000 | Allows simplified Tax Court procedures in interest-abatement cases |
| Tax Court judicial-conference fee | “Reasonable” registration fee; amount not set | May be used to defray conference expenses |

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 401** writes ten taxpayer rights into the Commissioner’s duties (informed, quality service, correct tax only, challenge and be heard, appeal, finality, privacy, confidentiality, representation, and a fair and just system).
- **Sec. 402** bars IRS officers and employees from using personal email for official business.
- **Sec. 404** requires an administrative appeal path for adverse exempt-status, private-foundation, and private-operating-foundation determinations, including those made on or after May 19, 2014.
- **Sec. 405** creates IRC section 506: a new 501(c)(4) must notify the IRS within 60 days of establishment (name, TIN, formation date and state, and purpose), with acknowledgment, a user fee, and the penalties above. Some existing organizations that had neither sought a determination nor filed a required return must notify within 180 days of enactment.
- **Sec. 406** extends Tax Court declaratory-judgment review to initial or continuing qualification of 501(c) organizations other than 501(c)(3), and to 501(d) organizations.
- **Sec. 407** makes termination of employment apply to performing, delaying, or failing to perform an official action—including an audit—for personal gain or a political purpose.
- **Sec. 408** provides that the gift tax does not apply to transfers of money or property to 501(c)(4), (5), or (6) organizations for gifts made after enactment, and states that this creates no inference about earlier transfers.
- **Sec. 409** lets the IRS require an identifying number, rather than a full Social Security number, on Form W–2.
- **Sec. 411** makes technical corrections to the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 partnership audit rules, including publicly traded partnership passive-loss adjustments and a limitations period of 330 days (plus any agreed extension) instead of 270 days.
- **Sec. 422** adds the $50,000 small-case election for interest-abatement petitions.
- **Secs. 431–432 and 441** require Tax Court judicial-conduct procedures, allow court-like administrative authorities and a judicial conference, and state that the Tax Court is not an executive-branch agency and is independent of that branch.

## Plain English

The IRS must follow a written list of taxpayer rights, social-welfare nonprofits must tell the IRS they exist, and people get clearer ways to challenge the IRS in Tax Court—without this title spending any new money.

## Title Summary

Title V contains no appropriations. It makes two trade-law changes: it resets the effective date of tariff-classification rules for recreational performance outerwear in the Trade Preferences Extension Act of 2015 (Public Law 114–27), and it amends the Bipartisan Congressional Trade Priorities and Accountability Act of 2015 (Public Law 114–26; 19 U.S.C. 4206) so the President may proclaim duty reductions on certain Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) environmental goods after notifying Congress.

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| No line items | None | This title authorizes no spending and sets no dollar amounts. |

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 501 — Outerwear classification date.** Replaces “the 180th day after the date of the enactment” (and “such 180th day”) in section 601(c) of Public Law 114–27 with **March 31, 2016**, delaying when those recreational performance outerwear tariff-classification rules take effect.
- **Sec. 502 — APEC environmental goods.** Adds subsection (c) to 19 U.S.C. 4206. Notwithstanding the notification rule in section 103(a)(2), the President may use proclamation authority under section 103(a)(1)(B) to implement an APEC agreement cutting duties on environmental goods listed in Annex C of the APEC Leaders Declaration of September 9, 2012—but only if, as soon as feasible after enactment and before using that authority, the President notifies Congress of the negotiations and the specific U.S. objectives.

## Plain English

This title spends no money; it postpones a clothing tariff-classification change until March 31, 2016, and lets the President lower tariffs on listed environmental goods if APEC members agree, after first telling Congress what the United States is seeking.

## Title Summary

Title VI does not appropriate money or fund any agency, bureau, or program. It is a budget-enforcement provision: Section 601 directs that the budgetary effects of the Act not be recorded on the statutory PAYGO scorecards under the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act of 2010, or on the Senate PAYGO scorecard under section 201 of S. Con. Res. 21 (110th Congress).

## Spending Breakdown

| Line Item | Amount | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| No appropriations or rescissions | None specified | This title contains no dollar amounts and provides no funding. |

## Notable Sections

- **Sec. 601(a) — Statutory PAYGO exemption.** Bars the Act’s costs from being entered on either PAYGO scorecard maintained under section 4(d) of the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act of 2010. Recording deficit increases on those scorecards can trigger across-the-board sequestration of certain mandatory spending.
- **Sec. 601(b) — Senate PAYGO exemption.** Bars the Act’s costs from being entered on any PAYGO scorecard kept for section 201 of S. Con. Res. 21 (110th Congress), the Senate’s pay-as-you-go rule.
- No new programs are created. The notable feature is the waiver of scorecard entry, which keeps the Act’s budgetary effects from counting toward those automatic budget-enforcement mechanisms.

## Plain English

This title says the cost of the law will not be counted on federal pay-as-you-go scorecards, so those costs will not by themselves trigger the automatic spending cuts those rules can require.
